tooley.q: In an optical fibre, the refractive index of the core is:
tooley.explain: n₁ > n₂ is required for total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary.
tooley.detail:
n₁ > n₂ is required (core index greater than cladding) so that light is totally reflected at the core-cladding boundary and kept in the core. If equal there is no optical boundary; if smaller the ray always refracts into the cladding and is lost.

Picture: high core, low cladding.

tooley.q: A suitable optical transmitter for use with an optical fibre is:
tooley.explain: The transmitter is an infrared LED or a low-power laser diode; the photodiode and phototransistor are receivers (Tooley 10.3).
tooley.detail:
The optical transmitter is an infrared LED or a low-power laser diode coupled directly to the fibre. The photodiode and phototransistor are receivers: they pass a large current when illuminated and a negligible one in the dark.

Transmit = LED/laser, receive = photodiode.

tooley.q: The typical core diameter for a monomode fibre is:
tooley.explain: Figure 10.5: single-mode core 5 µm, cladding 125 µm; multimode 50 µm.
tooley.detail:
Figure 10.5: a single-mode fibre has a core of about 5 µm (the order of the wavelength) and a 125 µm cladding, while multimode has a 50 µm core. The single-mode core is small so only one mode propagates. 125 µm is the cladding diameter, not the core.

Remember the pairs: 5/125 (single-mode) and 50/125 (multimode).

tooley.q: In a multicore fibre-optic cable:
tooley.explain: Tooley 10.4.1: the buffers are colour coded blue, red, green, yellow and white to identify the fibres.
tooley.detail:
Tooley 10.4.1: the protective buffer of each fibre is colour-coded (blue, red, green, yellow, white) to identify the fibres in the cable. The core and cladding are the glass inside so they cannot be coloured.

The cable's outer jacket is usually purple.

tooley.q: The typical wavelength of light in a fibre is:
tooley.explain: Near-infrared 1.3 µm (1310 nm), together with 0.85 and 1.55 µm.
tooley.detail:
Fibre uses near-infrared light, typically 1.3 µm (1310 nm), also 0.85 µm and 1.55 µm; these lie in the low-loss windows of silica fibre. 13 µm and 130 µm are far infrared, not used in fibre.

Units: 1.3 µm = 1300 nm.

tooley.q: What aircraft standard applies to fibre-optic networks?
tooley.explain: ARINC 636, adapted from FDDI, for the Boeing 777 AVLAN and CABLAN (up to 100 Mbps).
tooley.detail:
ARINC 636 (adapted from FDDI) is the standard for the Boeing 777's optical AVLAN and CABLAN, at up to 100 Mbps. ARINC 429 is a copper point-to-point bus and 573 is the flight data recorder standard.

Memory: 636 = optical network.

tooley.q: If a launcher has an acceptance angle of 45°, the corresponding numerical aperture will be:
tooley.explain: NA = sin θa = sin 45° = 0.707.
tooley.detail:
NA = sin θa = sin 45° = 0.707. 0.5 is sin 30° and 1 is sin 90° (θa = 90°, accepting every ray). The inverse: θa = sin⁻¹(NA).

Quick check: sin 45° = √2/2 ≈ 0.707.

tooley.q: The typical cladding diameter for a monomode fibre is:
tooley.explain: The cladding is 125 µm (Figure 10.5).
tooley.detail:
The cladding of a typical single-mode fibre is 125 µm (Figure 10.5). 5 µm is the single-mode core diameter and 50 µm the multimode core.

The common 125 µm size lets connectors be shared across fibre types.

tooley.q: If the numerical aperture of a fibre has a value of 1, this indicates that:
opts: all of the light from the source is captured by the fibre
none of the light from the source is captured by the fibre
50 per cent of the light from the source is captured by the fibre
tooley.explain: NA = 1 means θa = 90°: every ray from the source is captured (ideal).
tooley.detail:
NA = 1 corresponds to θa = 90° so every ray from the source lies in the acceptance cone and is captured (ideal). Only NA = 0 would capture nothing; 50% does not correspond to a specific NA value.

In practice a fibre's NA is only about 0.2 to 0.3.

tooley.q: When replacing a length of multi-way fibre-optic cable, it is essential to ensure that:
opts: none of the red band is covered when the coupling nut is tightened
all of the red band is covered when the coupling nut is tightened
the connectors are correctly aligned prior to mating the plug and the receptacle
tooley.explain: Align before mating. A correct connection has the red band at least 50% covered (not 0% or 100%).
tooley.detail:
When replacing multi-way cable the connectors must be correctly aligned before mating the plug and receptacle. A correct connection has the receptacle's red band at least 50% covered by the coupling nut, so "none covered" or "all covered" are not the required conditions.

Rule: the plug has a yellow band, the receptacle a red band.

tooley.q: In order to support a high data rate, a fibre-optic cable should have:
tooley.explain: Maximum data rate goes with bandwidth (Tooley 10.3).
tooley.detail:
Maximum data rate goes with bandwidth: the wider the bandwidth, the narrower the pulses that can be sent and the more bits per second. Zero or limited bandwidth would restrict the rate.

Tooley 10.3 links bandwidth with dispersion.

tooley.q: A significant advantage of fibre-optic networks in large passenger aircraft is:
tooley.explain: Reduced weight, saving up to about 1,300 kg.
tooley.detail:
A significant advantage of fibre on large aircraft is reduced weight: copper is about 5 times heavier, saving up to 1,300 kg. Installation cost is not lower (high precision needed) and maintenance is harder at connectors.

Drawbacks of fibre: precision, mechanical strength, bend radius.

tooley.q: A beam of light is incident at the critical angle at a boundary between two media of different refractive index. The emerging ray will travel:
tooley.explain: At θc, θr = 90°: the refracted ray runs along the boundary.
tooley.detail:
At the critical angle the refraction angle is 90° so the emerging ray runs along the boundary. Below the critical angle the refracted ray leaves the boundary into medium 2; above it there is total reflection back toward the source.

Three regions: below θc (refraction), at θc (along the boundary), above θc (TIR).

tooley.q: The bandwidth of an optical fibre is limited by:
opts: attenuation and cross-talk in the cable
the number and severity of bends in the cable
modal dispersion occurring in the cable
tooley.explain: Dispersion stretches pulses and sets the maximum bit rate (Tooley 10.3).
tooley.detail:
The bandwidth of a multimode fibre is limited by modal dispersion: modes travel different path lengths and arrive at different times, so pulses broaden and each bit must be longer. Attenuation sets distance rather than bandwidth, and bending causes power loss.

Dispersion limits bit rate; attenuation limits length.

tooley.q: Light propagates in a fibre optic by means of:
tooley.explain: A chain of total internal reflections at the core-cladding boundary.
tooley.detail:
Light propagates in a fibre by a chain of total internal reflections at the core-cladding boundary. Modal dispersion stretches pulses and is not a guiding mechanism; "continuous refraction" is how graded-index fibre guides, not the general answer.

TIR needs n₁ > n₂ and an incidence angle above the critical angle.

tooley.q: The attenuation of an optical fibre is typically:
opts: between 2 dB and 20 dB per km
tooley.explain: Tooley 10.2.2: good-quality fibre is below 2 dB/km at 1.3 µm (the lecture gives 0.2 to 0.5 dB/km at 1550 nm).
tooley.detail:
Tooley 10.2.2: a good-quality fibre has less than 2 dB/km at 1.3 µm, so 50 m of fibre loses about 0.1 dB. The lecture gives even smaller values: 0.2 to 0.5 dB/km at 1550 nm. The other two options are far too large for good fibre.

Watch out: the unit is dB per km.

tooley.q: The main advantage of monomode fibres is:
tooley.explain: No modal dispersion, so the highest bandwidth; in exchange for cost and harder splicing.
tooley.detail:
Single-mode fibre has no modal dispersion so it gives the highest bandwidth and data rate, in exchange for higher cost and harder cutting, splicing and alignment. So "cheaper" is wrong, and the cable is not smaller overall (the cladding is still 125 µm).

Tooley: slower multimode is still common on aircraft because it is easy to fit.

tooley.q: A pulse of infrared light travelling down a multimode fibre optic becomes stretched. This is due to:
tooley.explain: Modes travel different path lengths and so arrive at different times.
tooley.detail:
An infrared pulse stretched in a multimode fibre is due to dispersion: the modes travel different path lengths so they do not arrive together. Reflection and refraction are the guiding mechanisms and do not stretch pulses.

Consequence: a limit on the bit rate.

tooley.q: Attenuation in an optical fibre is due to:
tooley.explain: Absorption, scattering (in the core and at the boundary) and radiation at bends (Tooley 10.2.2). Dispersion is a different effect.
tooley.detail:
Attenuation is due to absorption, scattering (in the core and at the core-cladding boundary) and radiation at bends in the fibre (Tooley 10.2.2). Dispersion is a different effect (pulse stretching); crosstalk and noise belong to electrical systems, not to power loss in the fibre.

The attenuation coefficient counts only the fibre's own loss, not coupling or bending.

tooley.q: Light waves in fibre-optic cables are:
tooley.explain: 850, 1310, 1550 nm are all near-infrared, so not visible.
tooley.detail:
850, 1310 and 1550 nm are all near-infrared so the light in fibre cables is not visible. Because it is invisible, the cable must be disconnected at both ends before looking at a connector face: the eye's blink reflex does not protect it.

The visible spectrum is only about 400 to 700 nm.

floyd.q: Which data transmission media does Floyd list?
opts: Only optical fiber cable, radio waves and satellite links
Wire, coaxial cable, twisted pair cable, optical fiber cable, and wireless
Only wire, coaxial cable and shielded twisted pair cable
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.13 · Section 13-1 Checkup #1 (p.745; answer p.797)
floyd.detail:
Floyd 13-1: data transmission media include wire, coaxial cable, twisted-pair cable, optical fibre cable and wireless. The other two options list too few.

Optical fibre is one of five, covered in the later sections.

floyd.q: According to Floyd, what kind of fibre is 8.3/125 µm?
opts: Multimode, 125 µm core and 8.3 µm cladding
Multimode, 8.3 µm core and 125 µm cladding
Single-mode, 8.3 µm core and 125 µm cladding
floyd.explain: Floyd: 50/125 and 62.5/125 are multimode; 8.3/125 is single-mode (first number core, second cladding).
floyd.detail:
Floyd: 50/125 and 62.5/125 are multimode, 8.3/125 is single-mode; the first number is the core diameter, the second the cladding, in µm. Single-mode gives more bandwidth and distance but costs more.

Compared with Tooley Figure 10.5 (5/125) the single-mode core size differs slightly because it depends on the fibre.

floyd.q: What is the main disadvantage of fibre-optic data transmission according to Floyd?
opts: Lower data rate than ordinary coaxial cable
Susceptibility to EMI in the aircraft environment
Cost, higher than coax, UTP and STP
floyd.explain: Floyd p.742: fibre is not susceptible to EMI and is faster; the main disadvantage is cost.
floyd.detail:
Floyd p.742: fibre is faster, has higher signal capacity, transmits farther and is immune to EMI; the main disadvantage is a cost higher than coax, UTP and STP. The other two options reverse the facts (fibre is immune to EMI and faster).

Same as Tooley 10.1: the difficulty lies in installation precision.

floyd.q: Which Floyd connector is duplex, holding two fibres for two-way communication?
floyd.explain: Floyd: ST is common for multimode, MT is a 12-fibre ribbon connector, FDDI is duplex.
floyd.detail:
Floyd lists ST, SC, FC, LC, LX-5, MT and FDDI; the FDDI is duplex, holding two fibres for two-way communication. ST is common for multimode networks and MT is 12-fibre for ribbon cable.

Duplex = simultaneous two-way over two fibres.

floyd.q: Which description of single mode in an optical fibre matches Floyd's answer?
opts: Light travels as a single ray, the core is smaller than multimode, more bandwidth and distance but costlier
Light does not reflect but travels straight through the cladding, so no high-index core is needed
Light travels in many rays through a large core, with lower bandwidth and a lower price than multimode
floyd.detail:
Floyd's printed answer A-27: in single mode the light travels as a single straight ray, the core is smaller than multimode, giving more bandwidth and distance but a higher cost. The other options describe multimode or are wrong about the mechanism (light is always kept in the core).

Compare: multimode has many rays and time dispersion.

floyd.q: Unshielded twisted pair cables are used for indoor telephone applications.
floyd.detail:
UTP is widely used for indoor telephone, computer networks and USB; it is colour-coded to a standard 25-pair code and uses RJ-45 connectors. UTP suits low-noise environments and lower frequencies than coax (up to about 1 MHz); for more EMI protection use STP.

Compared with fibre: fibre is immune to EMI.

floyd.q: Crosstalk increases when twisted pairs are bundled together.
floyd.explain: False: crosstalk is minimised when twisted pairs are bundled together.
floyd.detail: The two wires in each pair are twisted so they cross at nearly 90° and the electromagnetic fields generated by the signals cancel. Self-Test 1: crosstalk is minimised by twisted-pair cables (answer (b)). Floyd chapter 13 Problem 3 (in the Module 09 free-response section) asks exactly this.

floyd.q: Optical fiber cables transmit light pulses through the fibers.
floyd.detail: Instead of electrical pulses over copper, fibre uses light pulses. Advantages: faster data rates, higher signal capacity, longer distance, immunity to EMI; the main drawback is cost. Common data rates are 10 to 40 GHz, some above 100 GHz (Floyd p.742).

floyd.q: Optical fibers are not suitable for networking.
floyd.explain: False: optical fibre is commonly used for telecommunication and networking.
floyd.detail: Because light propagates through the fibre with little attenuation compared with electrical cables, fibre is useful for long-distance transmission. The Boeing 777 was the first commercial aircraft with an optical-fibre LAN (AVLAN, CABLAN; Tooley 10.4).

floyd.q: Communication in the infrared region can be line-of-sight or diffused.
floyd.detail: Line-of-sight (LOS) infrared needs transmitter and receiver to see each other with no obstacles; diffused infrared reflects off nearby surfaces such as walls. Light in optical fibre is also near-infrared but is guided in the fibre so no LOS is needed.

floyd.q: Types of rf and microwave signals propagating through Earth's atmosphere are ground wave, ionospheric and line-of-sight.
floyd.detail: Ground waves follow Earth's curvature (up to about 2 MHz, like the AM band). Ionospheric waves (about 30 to 85 MHz) bounce off the ionosphere, as ham radio does. Line-of-sight needs mutual visibility, limited to about 100 km between ground stations. Self-Test 6: ham radio signals bounce off the ionosphere.

floyd.q: Advantages fibre-optic systems have over electrical transmission media are:
opts: a higher data rate, higher EMI and less distortion
a higher data rate, less susceptibility to noise and a longer transmission distance
lower cost, higher data rate and simplicity
floyd.detail:
The second option is wrong because fibre costs more and is less simple; the third is wrong because fibre is immune to EMI, not "higher EMI". Recall Tooley 10.1: light, wide bandwidth, low noise and crosstalk, low attenuation, reliable, electrically isolating.

Note the word "advantages".

floyd.q: The modes of light propagation in optical fibers are:
floyd.detail:
Simplex and duplex are data transmission modes by direction; synchronous and asynchronous are ways of timing. Multimode has many rays (time dispersion); single-mode has a much smaller core so light travels nearly straight.

The names are easy to confuse: "light propagation modes" versus "data transmission modes".

floyd.q: The electromagnetic spectrum does NOT include:
floyd.detail:
Sound waves are mechanical waves (they need a medium), not electromagnetic; Floyd also notes that sonar makes low-frequency sound waves outside the electromagnetic spectrum. UV, radio and microwaves are all electromagnetic. Fibre light is infrared, between microwaves and visible light.

Elimination question: note the NOT.
Night vision uses infrared; X-rays are a much shorter wavelength band; AM broadcasting uses low-frequency ground waves. Link: the optical signals in fibre and remote controls also use infrared.

generated.q: Compute the critical angle of a glass (n = 1.5) to air (n = 1.0) interface.
generated.explain: sin θc = 1/1.5 = 0.667, θc = 41.8° (Tooley Test Your Understanding 10.2).
generated.detail:
sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.0/1.5 = 0.667 so θc = 41.8° (Tooley TYU 10.2). 48.2° is 90° − 41.8°, the angle between the ray and the boundary; 66.7 confuses a percentage. From glass into air, a ray above 41.8° is totally reflected.

Demo 2 of Module 08 shows the refracted ray vanishing at 42°.

generated.q: A fibre has n₁ = 1.53 and n₂ = 1.50. The numerical aperture NA is:
generated.detail:
NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = √(2.3409 − 2.25) = √0.0909 = 0.3015. 0.9804 is n₂/n₁ (used for the critical angle) and 0.03 is the index difference. θa = sin⁻¹(0.3015) = 17.55°.

NA contains the square root of the difference of squares, not the difference of indices.

generated.q: With NA = 0.275, λ = 1300 nm and a 62.5 µm core, the normalised frequency V is closest to:
generated.detail:
V = π d NA / λ = π × 62.5×10⁻⁶ × 0.275 / 1300×10⁻⁹ = 41.54. 13.2 divides by an extra π; 83.1 doubles it by mixing up radius and diameter.

Note d is the core diameter, not the radius.

generated.q: With V = 41.5, about how many modes does a multimode step-index fibre carry?
generated.detail:
N ≈ V²/2 = 41.54²/2 = 1725/2 ≈ 863 modes. 41 is V itself and 1,725 is V² without the division by 2.

A large mode count means strong modal dispersion.

generated.q: The power budget for 1 mW in and 50 µW minimum out is:
generated.detail:
Budget = 10 log₁₀(1 mW/50 µW) = 10 log₁₀(20) = 13.01 dB. 20 dB writes the ratio 20 as dB, and 3 dB is only double.

Power in dB uses 10 log, not 20 log.

generated.q: With a 13 dB budget and 0.35 dB/km attenuation, the maximum fibre length is:
generated.detail:
L_max = 13.01 dB / 0.35 dB/km = 37.2 km. 4.6 km would result from 2.8 dB/km, and 13.0 km confuses the budget with the length.

It depends on the attenuation read from the graph: 0.18 dB/km (1550 nm) gives 72.3 km.

generated.q: Light goes from water (n ≈ 1.33) into air (n = 1.0). The refracted ray:
generated.explain: Entering a lower index gives θr > θi (slide 12). Tooley 10.2's opposite wording is wrong.
generated.detail:
Entering a lower index gives θr > θi: the ray bends away from the normal (slide 12). Tooley section 10.2 states the rule backwards so it should not be used for study. Example: water (1.33) into air at 30° gives sin θr = 1.33 × 0.5 = 0.665, θr = 41.7° > 30°.

High to low index: away; low to high: toward.

generated.q: The two lowest-attenuation wavelengths of silica fibre are about:
generated.explain: Slide 26: ≈ 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm and ≈ 0.18 dB/km at 1550 nm; 1.39 µm is the OH⁻ peak.
generated.detail:
Slide 26: loss minima ≈ 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm and ≈ 0.18 dB/km at 1550 nm, so most optical systems run at these two wavelengths. 1390 nm is the OH⁻ (water) absorption peak so it is avoided; 850 nm serves short multimode links.

Three windows: 850, 1310, 1550 nm.

generated.q: Which fibre type has the highest bandwidth?
generated.detail:
Single-mode fibre has the highest bandwidth because only one mode propagates, so there is no modal dispersion (slide 30). Multimode step-index has the lowest bandwidth, graded-index lies between.

Bandwidth order: SM > MM-GI > MM-SI.

generated.q: Six connectors, each with 0.5 dB loss. The total connector loss is:
generated.detail:
6 × 0.5 dB = 3 dB (Tooley 10.4.2), equal to several kilometres of low-loss fibre. dB can be added because dB is a logarithmic scale of a ratio: losses in series add.

0.5 dB means losing about 11% of the power at each connector.

generated.q: A 20 dB power loss means the remaining power is what fraction of the original?
generated.detail:
10^(−20/10) = 10⁻² = 0.01: losing 20 dB leaves 1% of the power. 0.1 is the result of −10 dB and 0.5 of −3 dB.

In amplitude (voltage) terms −20 dB is a factor of 0.1.

generated.q: With n₁ = 1.48 and n₂ = 1.46, the critical angle θc at the core-cladding boundary is about:
generated.detail:
The index difference is only 0.02 so θc is very close to 90°: the ray must be almost parallel to the axis to be totally reflected. 9.4° = 90° − 80.6° is the angle between ray and axis; 45° would hold only if n₂/n₁ = 0.707.

A small index difference means a narrow acceptance cone.

generated.q: For a fibre with n₁ = 1.48, n₂ = 1.46 in air, the numerical aperture NA is:
generated.detail:
1.48² = 2.1904 and 1.46² = 2.1316, difference 0.0588, root = 0.2425 (rounds to 0.242). θa = sin⁻¹(0.2425) = 14.0°. 0.02 is the index difference and 0.986 is n₂/n₁.

NA describes light-gathering ability.

generated.q: A step-index multimode fibre with NA = 0.20 at 850 nm carries about 1000 modes. The core diameter is about:
generated.detail:
From N ≈ V²/2, V = √(2 × 1000) = 44.72. From V = (2π a/λ) NA, a = Vλ/(2π NA) = 44.72 × 0.85 µm/(2π × 0.20) = 30.25 µm; d = 2a = 60.5 µm, close to the answer on slide 36. 6.05 µm and 605 µm are off by a factor of 10.

This is the lecture's slide 36 exercise.

generated.q: The same fibre (a = 30.25 µm, NA = 0.20) at 1550 nm has a normalised frequency V and mode count of about:
generated.detail:
A longer wavelength gives a smaller V: V is inversely proportional to λ. At 1320 nm V = 28.8 and M ≈ 414; at 850 nm V = 44.7 and M = 1000. The third option mixes the V of 1320 nm with the M of 1550 nm and the second is V at 850 nm.

Slide 36: at 1550 nm V ≈ 24.5 and M ≈ 301.

generated.q: A fibre has 0.18 dB/km, 1 mW input and a minimum detectable power of 50 µW. The maximum length is about:
generated.detail:
The same 13.01 dB budget with lower attenuation goes farther. 37.2 km is the result at 0.35 dB/km (1310 nm) and 7.2 km is off by a factor of 10.

So state the α you used when handing in the slide 27 exercise.

generated.q: With 2 mW input, after a 10 km fibre section of 0.2 dB/km the output power is:
generated.detail:
A = 0.2 dB/km × 10 km = 2 dB. P_out = P_in × 10^(−2/10) = 2 × 0.631 = 1.26 mW. 1.0 mW would be a 3 dB loss; 0.02 mW would be 20 dB.

Remember: 3 dB ≈ half the power, 10 dB ≈ one tenth.

generated.q: In a multimode fibre, modal dispersion for the critical ray is given by the correct formula:
generated.explain: The critical ray travels L/sin θc = L n₁/n₂.
generated.detail:
The axial ray travels L in a time n₁L/c; the critical ray travels L n₁/n₂ so it takes n₁²L/(n₂c). The difference: Δt = n₁L/c × (n₁/n₂ − 1) = n₁(n₁ − n₂)L/(c n₂). Slide 28 writes (n₁ − n₂)L/c, missing the factor n₁/n₂ (≈ 1.01 to 1.03, a small difference). With n₁ − n₂ = 0.02 to 0.04 it gives about 67 to 137 ns/km, not 10 to 50 ns/km.

Checked in code in the notebook.

generated.q: The conversion between attenuation in dB/km and in Np/km is:
generated.detail:
P(L)/P(0) = e^(−αL) so 10 log₁₀ of it equals −4.343 αL. Example: 0.35 dB/km corresponds to α = 0.0806 Np/km. 0.115 is the inverse factor (1/8.686 for amplitude, not power).

Tooley section 10.2.2: the attenuation coefficient counts only the fibre's own loss.

generated.q: How does graded-index multimode fibre compare with step-index?
opts: Lower modal dispersion and higher bandwidth
generated.explain: Slide 30: MM-GI has a parabolic profile, lower dispersion than MM-SI.
generated.detail:
In graded-index fibre, rays far from the axis travel in a lower-index region so they run faster, compensating for the longer path, so the modes arrive nearly together. Only one mode is single-mode fibre. The slide's label (MM-SI) on the middle column is a mistake: the correct label is MM-GI.

Bandwidth order: SM > MM-GI > MM-SI.

generated.q: The typical fibre-optic cable in Tooley 10.4.1 comprises:
opts: Two optical fibres and five fillers
Five optical fibres and two filler strands, separator tape, aramid yarn, outer jacket
generated.explain: 5 + 2: five light-carrying fibres, two fillers to keep the shape.
generated.detail:
The polyester fillers hold the cable shape, polyester tape makes it flexible, aramid (Kevlar) yarn carries tension, and the thermoplastic jacket (usually purple) resists moisture and insulates. Each fibre has a colour-coded buffer (blue, red, green, yellow, white).

Lecture slide 31 draws the same structure.

generated.q: Which sign shows an optical connector has been mated correctly?
opts: No colour band is visible any more
The receptacle's red band is at least 50% covered by the coupling nut
The plug's yellow band is completely covered by the receptacle
generated.explain: Tooley 10.4.2: a correct connection is made when the red band is at least 50% covered.
generated.detail:
The plug's coupling nut has a yellow band and the receptacle a red band. The 50% covering position indicates that the fibres in the plug are aligned end to end with those in the receptacle. Over-tightening can damage the fibres so the plug's guide pins act as a buffer stop.

The three start threads ensure a straight start.

generated.q: Why must the cable be disconnected at both ends before examining an optical connector face?
opts: Because the connector carries a high voltage
Because the infrared light is invisible and can be intense enough to cause permanent eye damage
generated.detail:
The eye cannot see infrared so the blink reflex does not protect it. Fibre carries no high voltage and does not melt at communication power levels.

Safety rule: never look into a fibre end or connector connected to a source.

generated.q: The Boeing 777 was the first commercial aircraft with an optical-fibre LAN. What are the two networks?
generated.explain: Tooley 10.4: AVLAN in the flight deck and electrical equipment bay, CABLAN in the cabin roof.
generated.detail:
Both follow ARINC 636, adapted from FDDI to reach 100 Mbps. AFDX is the switched Ethernet of the A380/A350 (Module 05) and CAN is an automotive bus.

FDDI is the origin of the standard, not the network's name.

generated.q: In a bypass switch unit (BSU) of the optical ring, what does a logic HIGH on PRI HI or SEC HI do?
opts: Disconnects the BSU from the ring
Connects the BSU to the fibre-optic ring
generated.explain: Tooley 10.5: HIGH = connect; LOW = disconnect; PRI RTN and SEC RTN are grounds (active low).
generated.detail:
The router sends four control signals to the BSU: PRI HI, PRI RTN, SEC HI, SEC RTN. The fibre-optic interface converts the BSU's optical signals to electrical ones and vice versa. A LOW on HI disconnects the BSU so the ring keeps running when that node fails.

This is a redundancy mechanism for a ring network.

generated.q: In the fibre-optic link block diagram (Floyd Figure 13-8), which block converts light back into an electrical signal?
opts: The light-to-electrical converter at the receiver
The electrical-to-light converter at the transmitter
generated.explain: Figure 13-8: electrical source → electrical-to-light → fibre cable → light-to-electrical → receiver.
generated.detail:
At the transmitter the electrical signal modulates the light intensity; at the receiver a photodiode converts it back. Connectors only couple light in or out of the cable. The printed answer to chapter 13 Problem 7 is Figure P-100 with the same blocks.

Transmit: LED or laser; receive: photodiode.
